newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary committee to focus on EMU, not punt.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary committee to focus on EMU, not punt.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee meets on Friday amid rife market speculation of a possible revaluation of the Irish punt, but officials say there are no plans to discuss the currency's continued rise.

The meeting of national treasury and central bank officials will focus instead on a number of issues pertaining to economic and monetary union, in particular future relations between EU finance ministers and a European Central Bank.
EU monetary officials on Wednesday said the Irish economy's fundamentals did not justify a revaluation of the punt.
"There is no intention whatsoever to talk about the Irish punt," a senior EU official told Reuters.
The meeting will also discuss the relationship between the euro and currencies such as dollar, as well as the impact EMU will have on the International Monetary Fund.
Another point on the agenda is how the monetary committee will eventually evolve into the so-called Economic and Financial Committee after the euro is launched.

On the Irish punt, a number of monetary sources believe that revaluing it could prompt unwanted turbulence within Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism, a system of keeping major currencies aligned to one another.

With the punt's strength stemming primarily from the rise in sterling and the dollar, a revaluation would run the risk of a sharp decline in the punt once the other two currencies reversed course, officials say.
Typically, the committee gathers on a weekend to consider any changes to the ERM.
EU officials on Thursday also said there were no plans to discuss the fixing of conversion rates for currencies entering monetary union.
"It's certainly not on the agenda," said one official, adding that the matter would be taken up by the group when they meet again on September 3.
EU finance ministers are scheduled to meet informally in Luxembourg on September 13 to discuss ways of minimising currency speculation ahead of the euro's introduction on January 1, 1999.
